campanula-medium.summary: Canterbury bells usually spends its first year as a leafy rosette, then sends up a tall stem lined with generous bell-shaped flowers. Blue, pink, purple and white garden forms make this European biennial a familiar cottage-garden plant. The lower leaves are long and toothed, with smaller leaves along the flowering stem. Seed escapes through small openings in the dry capsules, allowing new plants to appear nearby. Deadhead before capsules mature if you want to keep the display within its chosen bed.

nymphaea-capensis.summary: Cape blue waterlily holds its fragrant flowers above a raft of broad floating leaves. Although blue is the familiar color, named forms and cultivated relatives can also flower pink or mauve. The leaves have a deep notch and a wavy edge, while a short upright, tuberous rhizome anchors the plant below. It comes from Africa and grows in still or slow water. Keep pond plants and discarded rhizomes out of natural waterways, and use more than flower color to distinguish this species from waterlily hybrids.

tecoma-capensis.summary: Cape honeysuckle is a scrambling southern African shrub with clusters of bright trumpet flowers. It belongs to the trumpetvine family, and its compound leaves—usually with five to nine toothed leaflets—help distinguish it from true honeysuckles. Orange-red is typical, with yellow and other colors available in garden selections. Long capsules release winged seeds, and stems can be propagated by layering or cuttings. Give a planting room, prune it to the intended space, and keep rooted trimmings from being dumped beyond the garden.

plumbago-auriculata.summary: Cape leadwort is a loose, scrambling shrub covered in clusters of pale blue flowers, with white-flowered selections also grown. Its small light-green leaves have little ear-shaped appendages near the base, a useful detail behind the name auriculata. Native to southern Africa, it is widely planted in warm gardens and can become a broad mass without pruning. Sunny conditions and good drainage suit it well. Keep a planting within its intended area and collect trimmings rather than dropping them at the edge of natural vegetation.

crassula-multicava.summary: Fairy crassula spreads as a low succulent mat, with fleshy rounded leaves and airy clusters of small pale pink stars. Tiny plantlets may form among the flowers, drop to the ground, and become new plants; creeping stems also root where they touch soil. That easy propagation makes garden waste an effective way to start another patch. The South African species has become an environmental weed in parts of Australia and New Zealand. Collect every loose piece during removal and revisit the site for rooted fragments or fallen plantlets.

stipa-capensis.summary: Cape ricegrass is easiest to notice when its seed heads develop long, twisted awns. These bristles give the annual grass a tangled appearance and help its sharp seeds catch on clothing or animal fur. Narrow leaves and a compact seed head support identification, but flowering material is especially useful. In southern California desert areas, it can form dense patches and is a concern for native wildflowers and fire potential. Brush seeds from footwear before leaving a patch and report unfamiliar stands to the local land manager.

sources.label: Stipellula capensis: GrassBase and Flora of Oman

delairea-odorata.summary: Cape ivy can drape a streambank or woodland edge in a thick green blanket. Its fleshy, lobed leaves resemble ivy, but clusters of tiny yellow flower heads reveal its place in the daisy family. In invaded coastal California habitats, the vine climbs over shrubs and trees and shades the plants beneath. Even small stem and underground pieces can start again after removal. Keep cut material out of waterways, collect fragments carefully, and expect repeated visits to clear regrowth rather than a single successful pull.

arctotheca-calendula.summary: Fertile capeweed spreads a rosette of deeply lobed leaves close to the ground, then lifts yellow daisy heads with dark centers above it. Turn a leaf over to see the pale, woolly underside. This seed-producing species is an agricultural and environmental weed in parts of Australia and has established in coastal California. Its seeds travel with soil, equipment, footwear, and animals. Remove small plants before seed ripens and check the identification carefully: the creeping ornamental capeweed, Arctotheca prostrata, has different spreading habits and yellow flower centers.

arctotheca-prostrata.summary: Creeping capeweed was planted as a groundcover for its low rosettes and cheerful yellow daisies, but its runners can cross the intended boundary. Stems root as they creep, allowing a patch to expand even where the cultivated plants produce no fertile seed. California records describe escapes into coastal prairie and nearby urban ground. It is often confused with fertile capeweed, Arctotheca calendula; longer creeping stems and yellow flower centers help separate it. During removal, collect rooted runners and fragments so the cleared patch can stay clear.

hydrochoerus-hydrochaeris.summary: Capybaras are the largest living rodents, with sturdy brown bodies, blunt muzzles, and short legs adapted to life beside water. Partly webbed feet and eyes, ears, and nostrils set high on the head help them swim while keeping watch. In their South American range, they live socially and graze on grasses and aquatic plants. An animal seen far outside that range may be an escape or release. Observe from a distance, keep pets away, and report the location to wildlife authorities rather than feeding or relocating it.

wigandia-urens.summary: Wigandia is a large-leaved shrub or small tree from tropical America, with showy lavender flowers above coarse, hairy foliage. The hairs are a reason to admire it without brushing past: they can irritate skin and sometimes provoke a stronger allergic reaction. Plants described from the Santa Monica Mountains have escaped cultivation into dense colonies near homes. Their big, toothed leaves and curling flower clusters give a useful starting point for identification, although local forms and older botanical names need careful comparison.

sources.label: Wigandia urens var. caracasana — Prigge and Gibson flora
Wigandia urens — University of Lisbon ISA

carum-carvi.summary: Caraway is the familiar kitchen spice grown on a delicate-looking member of the carrot family. Finely divided leaves form below branched stems topped with small white or pink-tinged flower umbels; the aromatic, ridged fruits are commonly called seeds. It often grows as a biennial and can self-sow freely where conditions suit it. In a herb bed, harvest or remove ripening heads to limit volunteers. Wild carrot-family plants can be difficult to tell apart, so do not use a casual resemblance as a basis for foraging.

cynara-cardunculus.summary: Cardoon brings the artichoke family’s bold outline to open ground: a broad rosette of deeply cut, gray-green leaves sends up tall stems topped with purple flower heads. This Mediterranean perennial is cultivated as a vegetable and ornamental, but wild plants also occupy California grasslands and other disturbed habitats. Its spiny leaves and substantial taproot make established plants awkward to remove. Seed and surviving root pieces can renew a patch, so a single cut rarely settles the problem.

saissetia-neglecta.summary: Caribbean black scale can look like a row of small dark bumps along a fruit stem or twig. Mature females develop a tough, rounded covering with an H-shaped ridge; younger scales are paler and less distinctive. This sap-feeding insect uses many plants, including citrus, mango and guava. On citrus, its sugary honeydew supports sooty mold that can reduce fruit quality. Tiny natural enemies help limit populations, making a close inspection more useful than an automatic spray.

sources.label: Soft Scale Insects of Florida Citrus — UF/IFAS

anastrepha-suspensa.summary: Caribbean fruit fly is a yellow-brown fly whose patterned wings offer a useful first clue to its identity. Females place eggs beneath the skin of mature or overripe fruit, and the pale larvae feed inside before dropping to the soil to pupate. Guava, loquat and many other cultivated or wild fruits can serve as hosts. Because related fruit flies look similar and have different management implications, a suspected find deserves expert identification before fruit is moved.

sources.label: Caribbean Fruit Fly Pest Profile — CDFA

tabebuia-aurea.summary: Silver trumpet tree pairs golden, funnel-shaped flowers with foliage that catches the light in a silvery sheen. Native to South America, it is planted as a warm-climate ornamental and may lose some or all of its leaves seasonally. The leaves spread from a single point like fingers, while mature capsules split to release winged seeds. Several yellow-flowered trumpet trees share this general silhouette, so the smooth leaflet edges and tiny surface scales are useful details to check.

sources.label: Silver Trumpet Tree — Hong Kong Greening

caucalis-platycarpos.summary: Small white flower clusters make bur parsley easy to overlook until its hooked fruits catch your attention. This annual has finely divided leaves and only a few rays in each flower cluster. It belongs to the flora of Europe, northern Africa and parts of Asia, where it often grows in dry cultivated ground and field margins. Its conservation context matters: Switzerland regards it as vulnerable. A plant found among crops is therefore not automatically a candidate for removal.

sources.label: Caucalis platycarpos — Kew, Flora of Iraq account

cupaniopsis-anacardioides.summary: Carrotwood’s glossy, leathery leaflets give this evergreen tree a tidy appearance, but its orange capsules reveal the feature that helps it travel: dark seeds wrapped in a bright aril that attracts birds. It is native to coastal eastern Australia, including rainforest near the sea and estuaries. In Florida, escaped trees invade a wide range of habitats and alter the understory. Young seedlings are much easier to tackle than the established trees they can become.

sources.label: Carrotwood — UF/IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants

tinea-pellionella.summary: The casemaking clothes moth’s most revealing sign is often a tiny moving case rather than a moth. Its caterpillar builds a portable shelter from silk and fibers, feeding on vulnerable animal-based materials such as wool as it carries the case along. The adult is a small, buff moth with narrow, fringed wings and dark forewing spots. Stored textiles and the sheltered undersides of wool rugs deserve attention, especially when they have gone undisturbed for a long time.

sources.label: Clothes Moths — University of Maryland Extension

senna-spectabilis.summary: Spectacular cassia earns its common name with broad clusters of bright yellow flowers above a rounded crown. This tropical American tree has compound leaves and long pods that darken as they mature. Its appeal as an ornamental has carried it beyond its native range; in parts of East Africa and India, it has spread into forest edges, gaps and degraded land. Dense growth can hinder forest recovery, so seedlings near vulnerable habitat merit attention before they become seed-bearing trees.

sources.label: Reproductive biology of Senna spectabilis — Journal of Threatened Taxa

manihot-esculenta.summary: Cassava is a tropical crop grown for its large, starch-rich storage roots, also familiar as the source of tapioca. Above ground, it forms a woody shrub with long-stalked, deeply divided leaves and milky sap. Farmers commonly propagate it from stem cuttings, a useful reminder that discarded stems can remain planting material. Although cassava is an important food plant, its raw parts contain toxins and require proper processing; the appearance of an edible crop does not make it safe to sample.

ricinus-communis.summary: Castor bean is hard to miss: huge, star-shaped leaves rise on fast-growing stems, followed by clusters of prickly capsules. In warm climates it can become a substantial shrub, while frost-prone gardens often grow it as an annual. Escaped plants favor disturbed ground and waterways, and mature capsules scatter seeds that can establish new plants. Those attractive, mottled seeds are highly poisonous, so this is a plant to identify visually and keep away from children and animals.

dolichandra-unguis-cati.summary: Cat’s-claw creeper climbs with tiny, three-pronged hooks that grip bark and other supports. Its yellow trumpet flowers may look inviting, but the woody vine can spread across forest floors and climb over trees, smothering vegetation in invaded areas. Underground tubers make it persistent after the visible stems are cut. Winged seeds travel by wind and water, while detached stems and tubers can also restart growth. Early identification is especially valuable around streambanks and woodland edges.

kalanchoe-pinnata.summary: Life plant has an unusual way of making a new generation: tiny plantlets can grow from the scalloped margins of its fleshy leaves, particularly after a leaf falls. This Madagascar succulent becomes an upright, shrubby perennial, with simple lower leaves and divided leaves farther up the stems. Drooping, bell-shaped flowers hang in branching clusters. Its easy propagation explains both its popularity and its tendency to become weedy; a discarded leaf can be more than garden litter.

sources.label: Mother of millions: resurrection plant comparison — NSW WeedWise

nepeta-cataria.summary: Catnip’s gray-green, aromatic leaves are familiar to many cat owners, but this mint-family perennial also attracts a lively mix of flower visitors. Small white flowers, often marked with pink or purple, crowd the tops of its square stems. Native to Europe and Asia, it has naturalized widely in temperate regions, especially along roadsides and field margins. It readily seeds around gardens and can become a nuisance, although that does not make every patch an ecological invasion.

bothriochloa-bladhii.summary: Caucasian bluestem forms dense clumps of pale green grass that turn straw-colored as they mature. Its branched seed head has a central axis extending beyond the shorter side branches, a helpful clue when comparing it with other bluestems. This warm-season perennial occurs under several regional common names, including forest blue grass in Australia. In Kansas, introduced stands have spread into native sites. Identification deserves care because the name “bluestem” also belongs to valuable native prairie grasses.

sources.label: Rangeland and Pasture Grasses of Kansas — K-State Research and Extension

phedimus-spurius.summary: Two-row stonecrop makes a low carpet of fleshy leaves, with creeping stems that root as they spread. Clusters of star-shaped pink or white flowers rise just above the mat, and many garden forms develop reddish foliage as the season changes. This perennial comes from the region around the Caucasus, northeastern Turkey and northern Iran, and is often sold under its older name, Sedum spurium. It tolerates dry, rocky ground well, which helps explain its popularity in rock gardens and planted roofs.

stachytarpheta-cayennensis.summary: Nettleleaf porterweed holds small blue-purple flowers along slender, curved spikes that rise above its wrinkled green leaves. Only part of a spike blooms at once, leaving a patterned stem behind as flowers fall. This tropical American shrub is grown ornamentally, but can spread through disturbed ground and degraded pasture in warm, moist regions. Seeds travel with contaminated soil, hay, equipment and garden waste. Other porterweeds are similar, making leaf texture and growth habit useful starting points rather than a final diagnosis.

colombian-datura-virus.summary: Colombian datura virus can hide in an apparently healthy angel’s trumpet, then show itself as pale mottling, wrinkled leaves or stunted growth. Brugmansia plants are important hosts, and moving infected cuttings helps carry the virus between collections. Aphids and transferred plant sap can spread it too. Related ornamental and crop plants can also be infected, including tomato. Because these symptoms overlap with other problems and some infected plants show none, reliable identification depends on laboratory testing.

sources.label: Colombian datura virus pest rating proposal — CDFA
First Report of Colombian datura virus in Brugmansia in Canada — Rott et al.

acacia-elata.summary: Cedar wattle is a tall Australian tree with unusually large leaflets for a feathery-leaved acacia. Sprays of pale yellow or cream flower balls appear above the foliage, followed by flat pods. In its native New South Wales range, it grows in rainforest and wetter eucalypt forest. Planting has carried it farther afield: it can escape into adjacent bushland and is documented as naturalized in South Africa. Its location matters when deciding whether a seedling belongs or needs attention.

sources.label: SAPIA News 8: alien Acacia identification key

chelidonium-majus.summary: Greater celandine brings small yellow flowers to shady edges, gardens, and disturbed woodland. This leafy herb lives for more than one season or behaves as a biennial, spreading readily by seed where conditions suit it. Its deeply divided leaves and orange-yellow sap help separate it from other yellow-flowered plants. Originally from Eurasia, it has become established beyond its native range. The sap can irritate skin, so this is a plant to recognize without breaking its stems by hand.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Chelidonium majus

pholcus-manueli.summary: This cellar spider belongs to the long-legged spiders that hang beneath loose webs in sheltered corners. Pholcus manueli has been recorded in cellars and other buildings, including a garage from which it was first described. Although its name was established from American specimens, the World Spider Catalog treats it as an Asian species introduced to the United States. Several cellar spiders look similar, so a web in a basement is a useful clue, not enough to identify this particular species.

sources.label: USDA Forest Service: Spiders of Milbridge, Maine

eremochloa-ophiuroides.summary: Centipedegrass is the pale-green, low-growing lawn grass often planted in warm parts of the country. It creeps across the soil on aboveground runners, gradually forming a coarse-textured turf rather than an upright clump. Its leaves alternate along the runners, giving them the appearance that inspired its common name. This grass is adapted to acidic, relatively low-fertility soils. Because it is widely cultivated, a patch beside a lawn should be described in that context rather than automatically labeled a harmful invasion.

sources.label: UF/IFAS: Identification of Common Florida Lawn Grasses

epipremnum-pinnatum.summary: Centipede tongavine is a tropical climbing plant whose leaves change dramatically as it grows. Young shoots creep or climb with relatively simple leaves; older shoots supported by a tree or another surface can produce much larger, deeply divided leaves. Aerial roots help the vine hold on as it climbs. Native across parts of Asia and the Pacific, it is grown ornamentally beyond that range. Its changing leaf shape makes identifying mature and juvenile plants together especially useful.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Epipremnum pinnatum

actinocyclus-normanii-f-subsala.summary: This microscopic diatom is known from freshwater plankton and is associated with the smaller freshwater forms of Actinocyclus normanii. Viewed through a microscope, its round silica shell has a patterned surface of pores that specialists use for identification. Its history in the Great Lakes is less straightforward than an introduction date might suggest: older sediment evidence has raised questions about whether it arrived recently at all. Even the boundary between named forms is uncertain, making careful identification more useful than a simple invasive label.

sources.label: Diatoms of North America: Actinocyclus normanii
USGS Great Lakes account: Actinocyclus normanii f. subsalsa

skeletonema-potamos.summary: Skeletonema potamos is a tiny diatom that drifts in fresh and slightly brackish water, often as short chains of cells. Its delicate silica walls are so small that it can be overlooked even under a light microscope. Researchers studying the Danube found that it became a larger part of the river's plankton community as water temperatures rose. Its original range remains uncertain, and finding it in a water sample does not by itself establish a harmful bloom or a recent introduction.

sources.label: USGS Great Lakes account: Skeletonema potamos
Duleba and colleagues: Skeletonema potamos in the River Danube

heterodera-avenae.summary: Cereal cyst nematode is a microscopic roundworm that feeds inside the roots of wheat, barley, oats, and other grasses. Damaged roots have more difficulty supplying the plant with water and nutrients, which can leave uneven patches of weak or stunted crop. After a female dies, her hardened body becomes a cyst that shelters eggs in the soil. Those persistent cysts make the problem longer-lived than one growing season, while the symptoms above ground can easily be mistaken for other crop stresses.

sources.label: Oregon State Extension: Cereal Cyst Nematodes

oulema-melanopus.summary: The cereal leaf beetle is a small insect with metallic blue wing covers and an orange-red area behind its head. Its larvae are easier to notice by what they leave behind: narrow strips of damaged tissue on cereal and grass leaves. A dark coating of their own waste often hides the larvae's pale bodies. Heavy feeding can reduce the leaf area a grain crop needs to fill its seeds, but natural enemies also help keep populations in check, making field monitoring important.

sources.label: Utah State University Extension: Cereal Leaf Beetle

secale-cereale.summary: Cereal rye is an upright annual grass grown for grain, forage, and soil cover. Its tall stems carry dense, bristly seed heads that may lean as they mature, while a network of roots helps hold the soil. It is a familiar agricultural plant that can also appear outside the places where it was sown. Despite the similar name, cereal rye is not the same as the ryegrasses used in many lawns and pastures. Identifying the seed head helps tell those grasses apart.

dianella-ensifolia.summary: Cerulean flaxlily forms clumps of long, sword-shaped leaves, with small pale flowers followed by glossy blue berries. Although its foliage may look grasslike at first glance, it spreads from underground rhizomes and carries its flowers on branching stalks above the leaves. Birds can disperse its fruit. Native across parts of the Old World tropics, it has also been grown as an ornamental. In Florida, UF/IFAS assesses it as invasive, so its attractive appearance should not be the only consideration when choosing a landscape plant.

cucumber-green-mottle-mosaic-virus.summary: Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus affects crops in the cucumber family, including cucumbers, melons, pumpkins, and squash. Infected plants may develop mottled or distorted leaves, poor growth, or damaged fruit, although symptoms vary with the crop and conditions. The virus travels with contaminated seed and plant material and can also move on hands, tools, and other surfaces. That combination makes clean planting material and careful hygiene especially important in gardens, greenhouses, and farms where susceptible crops are grown.

sources.label: USDA APHIS: Cucumber Green Mottle Mosaic Virus
Agriculture Victoria: Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus

phyllanthus-urinaria.summary: Chamberbitter is a small warm-season annual that can appear among garden plants, in lawns, and in other disturbed ground. Its neat rows of little leaves make a branch look like a miniature mimosa leaf, but those are individual leaves rather than leaflets. Turn a branch over and the round seed capsules underneath become a useful clue. Plants can make seed while still quite small, which is why repeatedly mowing the tops may leave the next generation ready to grow.

houttuynia-cordata.summary: Chameleon plant is a spreading perennial with heart-shaped leaves and a strong scent when its foliage is crushed. Garden forms may have brightly patterned leaves, but the plant can also be plain green. What look like four white petals surround a short spike of tiny flowers. It thrives in moist ground and spreads through creeping underground stems, which can carry it well beyond a garden bed. Those hidden stems also make an established patch more persistent than its soft leaves might suggest.

kalanchoe-delagoensis.summary: Chandelier plant is a succulent with narrow, mottled leaves and clusters of hanging orange-red flowers. Tiny plantlets develop at the leaf tips, detach, and become new plants, helping explain its other name, mother of millions. This Madagascar native has been grown ornamentally and can establish in warm, open habitats beyond gardens. Its ability to reproduce from small pieces makes garden waste an important concern. The plant is poisonous to livestock and pets, so identification matters around grazing land and homes.

myosotis-discolor.summary: Changing forget-me-not earns its name as its tiny flowers age from pale yellow or cream to blue. Several colors can appear on the same curling flower cluster, a helpful detail when this small plant blends into grassy ground. It is a hairy annual with slender stems and narrow leaves, originally from Europe and now established elsewhere. Roadsides, ditches, open pasture, and other disturbed places can provide suitable habitat. A close view of the flowers is much more useful for identification than a distant patch of blue.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Myosotis discolor

pomacea-canaliculata.summary: The channeled apple snail is a large freshwater snail that grazes on aquatic plants and can damage crops grown in wet fields. Its rounded shell has deep grooves between the coils, while conspicuous pink egg masses are laid above the waterline. Originally South American, it has been moved to other regions through human activity. In Hawaii, it became a serious pest of wetland taro. Several apple snails look alike, so shell color or a pink egg mass alone cannot settle the species identity.

sources.label: EPPO Global Database: Pomacea canaliculata datasheet
Levin and colleagues: Apple snails in Hawaii

sinapis-arvensis.summary: Charlock mustard, also called wild mustard, is an annual plant with clusters of bright yellow, four-petaled flowers. It often grows in cultivated fields and other disturbed ground, where its broad leaves and upright stems compete with crops for space and resources. Long seed pods follow the flowers, and seeds left in the soil can supply later generations. It belongs to the same plant family as many familiar vegetables, so recognizing its leaves, flowers, and pods together is more reliable than identifying it by color alone.

mytella-strigata.summary: The charru mussel is a small, thin-shelled mussel found in estuaries, lagoons, and other sheltered coastal waters. Its shell can range from greenish to nearly black, with a purple inner surface. It filters suspended food from the water and can gather on shells, roots, docks, and aquaculture structures. Introduced populations have become locally abundant, but abundance alone does not measure their effects: field research has found that competition with other mussels needs more careful study than some broad claims suggest.

sources.label: Wells and colleagues: Charru mussel in the upper Gulf of Thailand

sechium-edule.summary: Chayote is a vigorous climbing vine best known for its pale-green, pear-shaped vegetable, also called mirliton or vegetable pear. The fruit contains a single large seed, and the vine uses supports to lift its cucumber-like leaves and developing crop above the ground. Separate male and female flowers grow on the same plant and attract pollinators. This tropical American crop is cultivated in warm regions around the world. Its presence in a garden is therefore different from a vine growing independently beyond cultivation.

sources.label: Indian Institute of Science: Sechium edule

bromus-tectorum.summary: Cheatgrass is an annual grass that often starts growing in fall, spends winter as a small plant, and produces seed early the following season. Its soft, hairy leaves give way to drooping, bristly seed heads, then dry vegetation as the season warms. In many western landscapes, this early-drying growth adds fine fuel between larger plants and can help fires spread. Repeated disturbance can favor more cheatgrass, making prevention of seed production and recovery of perennial vegetation important parts of long-term management.

sources.label: Montana State Extension: Cheatgrass identification, biology and integrated management
